questions.q: Why do mature compliance programs avoid building a fully separate control implementation for each framework they're subject to?
options: Separate implementations are legally required by the frameworks themselves
It would multiply operational overhead — four audits each demanding fresh evidence for essentially the same underlying control
Auditors refuse to review organizations with more than one framework
Frameworks like SOC 2 and ISO 27001 cannot legally coexist at the same organization
questions.explain: Building one real control and mapping it across frameworks avoids recreating essentially the same access-review or logging process four separate times for four separate audits.

questions.q: In the quarterly access-review example, what makes one completed review useful across SOC 2, ISO 27001, and PCI DSS at once?
options: The review has to be performed three separate times, once per framework, to count
It only counts for whichever framework the organization audited first
The same evidence — a completed, signed-off review — maps to each framework's corresponding access-control requirement
Only SOC 2 actually requires access reviews; the others accept any arbitrary document
questions.explain: One quarterly access review, properly evidenced, can satisfy SOC 2's logical access criterion, ISO 27001's Annex A access-rights control, and PCI DSS's need-to-know access requirement simultaneously — the same underlying control, mapped three ways.

questions.q: What is a compliance control mapping, or crosswalk?
options: A record or table linking one internal control to the specific requirement it satisfies in each applicable framework
A legal filing submitted to a government regulator
A diagram of the organization's network topology
A list of every employee who has ever failed a phishing test
questions.explain: A crosswalk (often automated in GRC tooling) ties one control object to its corresponding requirement in each framework, so updating one piece of evidence can update compliance status across all of them.

questions.q: If one framework requires monthly access review and another mapped framework accepts quarterly, how should the underlying control actually be built?
options: To the quarterly cadence, since it's less work
To whichever cadence the newest framework requires, ignoring older mappings
Cadence doesn't matter as long as the mapping document exists
To the strictest cadence among all mapped frameworks — monthly in this case — not the most lenient one
questions.explain: A control mapped to multiple frameworks has to satisfy the most demanding requirement among them; building to the loosest cadence would leave the stricter framework's requirement unmet despite the mapping existing on paper.

questions.q: What is a genuine limit of control mapping, according to this lesson?
options: Mapping is a perfect universal translator and no framework ever has gaps a shared control misses
One framework may require more specific technical evidence, or a narrower/broader scope, than a general control actually captures
Crosswalks are purely illegal and auditors reject them outright
Only ISO 27001 can ever be mapped to another framework
questions.explain: Different evidence depth, different scope (e.g., a general access review vs. the specific Cardholder Data Environment), and different cadence requirements are real places where a single mapped control genuinely isn't sufficient on its own.
